## PDF page 23

```text
                            CHAPTER THREE



                   RANGE BUILDING


Poker is a game of incomplete information, and we will almost never know
the exact two hole cards our opponent has. But with logical deduction and
strong technical knowledge, building your opponent’s range becomes easier.

A range is simply a collection of all the possible hands a player could have
right this moment. We visualize a range using a 13x13 matrix that displays
all unique starting hands in Hold ‘em where pocket pairs form the diagonal,
suited combos are above the diagonal, and unsuited combos are below.




                                  PA G E 2 3
```

## PDF page 24

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/GTO/Poker-Math-Preflop-Workbook.pdf#page=24)

```text
                     P O K E R M AT H & P R E F L O P WO R K B O O K


It is important to note that ranges can be described multiple ways:

   1. A visual matrix, like the one you just saw

   2. The range strand. A string of text that describes the range of selected
     hands (i.e., AA-22,AT+,KJ+,QJs,JTs). This can be imported to and
     exported from your poker software

   3. The combo count. This adds together the combos of each hand
     selected in the matrix. We will explore combos in more detail later

   4. The %-form. When suits are considered, those 169 possible starting
     hands become 1,326 unique combos. There are 6 combos of AA which
     means the percentage form for just AA would be: AA = 6/1,326 = 0.45%

One of the best ways to improve your hand reading ability is to understand
how ranges, %-form, and frequencies interrelate. A frequency, or how often
your opponent does something, is just a percentage from 0% (they never do
something) to 100% (they always do something).

The best hand readers are paying careful attention to their opponent’s fre-
quencies (how often they open-raise from EP, how often they 3bet from the
button, how often they call 2bets from the CO, etc.) and correctly turning that
%-form into a usable range of hands. There are many nuances to doing this
well, but starting with the technical knowledge to go from %-form to a raw
range of hands gives you a massive leg up.

Given that this workbook is focused on math and preflop play, this section is
geared toward preflop ranges. We will explore postflop ranges more deeply
in an upcoming postflop workbook.

In this first part, you are going to explore the %-form for some common ranges.
The first 16 ranges are open-raising ranges, the following 12 are ranges that
```
